rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The opening of al-Fātiḥa is also the final wording of the supplications in 10:10, giving the sūra a return-to-the-beginning frame.
rows.anchor: وهو أول الفاتحة وآخر الدعوات الخاتمة كما قال تعالى

rows.speaker: الجنيد
rows.claim: Junayd was asked about the spiritual end and answered that it is returning to the beginning, an apt pattern for the sūra’s opening praise.
rows.anchor: قدس سره ما النهاية ؟ فقال الرجوع إلى البداية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In its familiar lexical sense, ḥamd is verbal praise of beauty, whether the praised excellence is an inherent virtue or a bestowed favor.
rows.anchor: والحمد على المشهور هو : الثناء باللسان على الجميل سواء تعلق بالفضائل أم بالفواضل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The act of ḥamd involves five elements: what is praised by, what is praised for, a praiser, a praised one, and an expression indicating the praised quality.
rows.anchor: قالوا ولا بد لتحققه من خمسة أمور : محمود به ومحمود عليه وحامد ومحمود

rows.speaker: الإمام الرازي
rows.claim: Al-Rāzī allows the praised quality to be positive or privative, transitive or intransitive, and voluntary or involuntary; al-Dawwānī and others endorse this account.
rows.anchor: لا فرق عند الإمام الرازي قدس سره بين كونه ثبوتيا أو سلبيا متعديا أو غير متعد

rows.speaker: العلامة في شرح التهذيب
rows.claim: A view reported and adopted in Sharḥ al-Tahdhīb requires the quality praised and the ground for praise to be voluntary.
rows.anchor: نقل عن البعض وجوب كونه اختياريا واختاره كما في المحمود عليه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The fact that people do not praise stature or a bright face, or that a pearl goes unpraised, cannot by itself prove whether the restriction lies in the praised quality or the ground for praise.
rows.anchor: لم يسمع الحمد على رشاقة القد وصباحة الخد لم يسمع الحمد بهما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The thing praised for is the cause of the praise: its excellence becomes manifest through the praised person’s possession of it; most scholars include both acts and enduring qualities.
rows.anchor: ظاهر كلام الجمهور أنه أعم من كونه فعلا صادرا من المحمود أو كيفية قائمة به

rows.speaker: الإمام الرازي
rows.claim: Al-Rāzī appears to restrict the ground of praise to an act performed voluntarily by the praised person.
rows.anchor: ويفهم كلام الإمام اختيار الأول ، واشترط أن يكون حصوله من المحمود باختياره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One quality can be both what a person is praised by and what they are praised for, as when someone is seen giving generously or praying; the two roles arise under different aspects.
rows.anchor: قد يكون الشيء الواحد محمودا به وعليه معا كأن رأي من ينعم أو يصلي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Praising God for essential attributes raises a problem if ḥamd requires voluntary acts, since those attributes may be identical with or additional to the divine essence.
rows.anchor: واستشكل الحمد على صفاته تعالى الذاتية سواء جعلت عين ذاته أو زائدة عليها

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: One solution treats praise of divine attributes as praise for what is effectively voluntary because God’s essence suffices for those attributes.
rows.anchor: وأجيب بأن الحمد عليها بتنزيلها منزلة الاختياري لكون ذاته كافية فيها

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Another solution defines voluntary action as action attributable to a free agent, whether or not that agent chose it in this instance.
rows.anchor: أو بأن المراد بالفعل الاختياري المنسوب إلى الفاعل المختار

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: A further view says divine attributes issue by choice in the sense that God would bring them about if He willed and would not if He did not, without making them temporally originated.
rows.anchor: وقيل : إنها صادرة بالاختيار بمعنى إن شاء فعل وإن لم يشأ لم يفعل

rows.speaker: الفلاسفة
rows.claim: Philosophers appeal to the distinction between a necessary conditional and the actuality of its antecedent, but al-Ālūsī argues that necessity leaves divine volition nominal or makes the world’s origin incompatible with their account.
rows.anchor: وقالوا إن صدق الشرطية لا يقتضي وجود مقدمها ولا عدمه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Ālūsī concludes that lexical ḥamd is praise for voluntary acts; praise of essential attributes is either figurative through their voluntary effects or conventional praise, both unobjectionable.
rows.anchor: والحق الحقيق بالاتباع أن الحمد اللغوي لا يكون إلا على الأفعال الاختيارية

rows.speaker: الصدر
rows.claim: The praiser must exalt the praised one through praise both outwardly and inwardly.
rows.anchor: أن يكون معظما بثنائه للمحمود ظاهرا وباطنا كما حققه الصدر

rows.speaker: المحققون
rows.claim: The discerning scholars do not require the praiser to believe the praised quality actually exists; it suffices that the description not accompany an assertion of contempt.
rows.anchor: لا يلزم اعتقاد اتصاف المحمود بالجميل عند المحققين ، بل الشرط عدم اقترانه ثبوت تحقير

rows.speaker: الدواني
rows.claim: Al-Dawwānī explains al-Sharīf’s requirement of inward and outward exaltation as intending the performative creation of esteem, not belief in a proposition.
rows.anchor: أراد بالاعتقاد لازمه ، وهو إنشاء التعظيم لا معناه الحقيقي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Ālūsī rejects the replies that a praiser must believe the literal description or must intend a metaphorical description; denial of a statement’s content does not prevent its rhetorical use.
rows.anchor: يرده أن الأول خلاف البديهة والثاني خلاف الواقع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The fifth element is an expression that manifests the praised one’s praiseworthiness; speech is conventionally singled out because the tongue is the usual instrument of speaking.
rows.anchor: وقد اشتهر تقييده باللسان وأريد به جارحة النطق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A person without a tongue can still praise through lip sounds or speech produced in another organ, as witnessed in a person lacking the whole tongue.
rows.anchor: فلو فقد إنسان لسانه فأثنى بحروفه الشفوية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qurʾānic statement that every thing glorifies God with praise shows that praise is not confined to utterance by a human tongue.
rows.anchor: وإن من شيء إلا يسبح بحمده

rows.speaker: الأكثر
rows.claim: Most scholars explain God’s self-praise as declaring His entitlement to praise, commanding praise, quoting the words of servants, or figuratively displaying His perfections; al-Sayyid favors the last account.
rows.anchor: فذهب الأكثر إلى أنه إخبار باستحقاق الحمد وأمر به أو مقول على ألسنة العباد

rows.speaker: الدواني
rows.claim: Al-Dawwānī considers figurative divine praise unnecessary because the people of truth affirm that God truly speaks; al-Ālūsī reads the tongue restriction as relative or customary.
rows.anchor: كون الحمد في حقه سبحانه مجازا بعيد عن قاعدة أهل الحق من إثبات الكلام له حقيقة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The lexical reality of ḥamd is manifesting perfection; spoken praise is merely its most obvious and familiar form, while manifestation through action is even fuller.
rows.anchor: فإن حقيقته عندهم إظهار صفات الكمال ، ولما كان الإظهار القولي أظهر أفراده

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One distinction is that ḥamd applies to voluntary actions of knowing beings, while madḥ also applies to involuntary qualities and nonrational things.
rows.anchor: أحدها : أن الحمد يختص بالثناء على الفعل الاختياري لذوي العلم ، والمدح يكون في الاختياري وغيره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ḥamd presupposes knowledge rather than conjecture and concerns complete qualities; madḥ may rest on conjecture or a pleasing but imperfect trait.
rows.anchor: وثانيها وثالثها : أن الحمد يشترط صدوره عن علم لا ظن ، وأن تكون الصفات المحمودة صفات كمال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ḥamd carries greater reverence and grandeur than madḥ, applies more particularly to rational beings and eminent persons, and is more often used of God.
rows.anchor: أن في الحمد من التعظيم والفخامة ما ليس في المدح

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ḥamd reports another’s virtues with love and reverence, so it combines information with an act of esteem; madḥ is bare information.
rows.anchor: أن الحمد إخبار عن محاسن الغير مع المحبة والإجلال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ḥamd is generally commanded, as in the saying that whoever does not thank people does not thank God, whereas madḥ is not universally praised and flatterers are rebuked.
rows.anchor: وسادسها : أن الحمد مأمور به مطلقا ففي الأثر : «من لم يحمد الناس لم يحمد الله »

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī appears to treat ḥamd and madḥ as synonymous; al-Ālūsī rejects that position and maintains that madḥ can praise what is involuntary.
rows.anchor: ويشعر كلام الزمخشري في «الكشاف والفائق » بترادفهما

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Some distinguish shukr from ḥamd by reserving shukr for bodily action and ḥamd for speech.
rows.anchor: خصه بالعمل والحمد بالقول

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Other definitions reserve shukr for apparent blessings or, alternatively, for inward blessings.
rows.anchor: جعله على النعم الظاهرة ، والآخر على النعم الباطنة

rows.speaker: الراغب
rows.claim: Al-Rāghib points to a definition of shukr as verbal expression for a blessing, while the familiar account includes grateful speech, service by the limbs, and belief and love in the heart.
rows.anchor: والمعروف أنه ما كان في مقابلتها قولا باللسان وعملا وخدمة بالأركان

rows.speaker: الطيبي
rows.claim: Al-Ṭībī says the technical usage of the legal theorists means worship, which is complete only through speech, bodily acts, and the heart.
rows.anchor: قول الطيبي إن هذا عرف أهل الأصول فإنهم يقولون شكر المنعم واجب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qurʾān 34:13 uses shukr for action, supporting the broader usage of gratitude beyond speech.
rows.anchor: اعملوا ءالَ دَاوُود شُكْراً

rows.speaker: النواس بن سمعان
rows.claim: Al-Ṭabarānī reports from al-Nawwās b. Samʿān that the Prophet vowed to thank God if his she-camel returned; when it did, he said al-ḥamdu lillāh, and the Companions expected further prayer or fasting.
rows.anchor: عن النواس بن سمعان : «أن ناقة رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم الجدعاء سرقت

rows.speaker: صاحب التجريد
rows.claim: The author of al-Tajrīd adds a fourth form of gratitude: thanking God by God, since no one but God can give Him His due thanks.
rows.anchor: وزاد بعضهم في أقسام الشكر رابعا وهو شكر الله تعالى بالله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: People generally recognize three modes of shukr; it overlaps with ḥamd in some respects, but ḥamd is its strongest branch because it openly discloses the blessing.
rows.anchor: والذي أطبق عليه الناس التثليث وعلى كل حال بينه وبين الحمد عموم وخصوص من وجه

rows.speaker: ابن عمر
rows.claim: A report from Ibn ʿUmar calls ḥamd the head of gratitude and says a servant has not thanked God unless he praises Him; al-Ālūsī notes its chain is interrupted.
rows.anchor: قال صلى الله عليه وسلم فيما رواه ابن عمر رضي الله تعالى عنهما : " الحمد رأس الشكر ما شكر الله تعالى عبد لا يحمده

rows.speaker: أنس
rows.claim: Al-Ālūsī cites a supporting report from Anas in which God tells Abraham that praise is the key to gratitude and gratitude ascends to the Lord of the Throne.
rows.anchor: إبراهيم سأل ربه فقال يا رب ما جزاء من حمدك؟ قال الحمد مفتاح الشكر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Calling ḥamd the head of gratitude suits its status as the most visible and principal form; this also explains why the Qurʾān opens with praise and begins the precious sūra with what is most precious.
rows.anchor: شبهه صلى الله عليه وسلم بالرأس الذي هو أظهر الأعضاء وأعلاها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Hamd is more elevated as worship than shukr because it need not be prompted by a benefit received, unlike gratitude for a gift.
rows.anchor: لو قال جل شأنه الشكر لله كان ثناء عليه تعالى بسبب إنعام وصل إلى ذلك القائل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An additional rationale is that shukr responds to finite gifts, while ḥamd can praise even for the unbounded benefit of averting harm, which is more urgent than gaining benefit.
rows.anchor: الشكر على الإعطاء وهو متناه والحمد يكون على المنع وهو غير متناه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In the common account, ḥamd has a limited means but a general object, whereas shukr has a general means but is directed specifically toward blessings.
rows.anchor: مورد الحمد في المشهور خاص ومتعلقه عام ، والشكر بالعكس موردا ومتعلقا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although tasbīḥ commonly precedes taḥmīd, the sūra omits it because praise includes declaring God free of defects while the reverse is not always true; tasbīḥ elsewhere serves a different purpose.
rows.anchor: التسبيح داخل في التحميد دون العكس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Tasbīḥ signals that God is free of defects, while ḥamd also points to His positive beneficence and the knowledge, power, and sufficiency that make it possible.
rows.anchor: والثاني يشير إلى كونه محسنا إلى العباد ولا يكون محسنا إليهم إلا إذا كان عالما قادرا غنيا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, every tasbīḥ is a kind of praise, but ḥamd is broader because it includes both negative and positive attributes while tasbīḥ addresses negative attributes.
rows.anchor: كل تسبيح حمد وليس كل حمد تسبيحا لأن التسبيح يكون بالصفات السلبية فحسب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Ālūsī takes the article in al-ḥamdu as generic: it points to the familiar notion of praise, as in Labīd’s verse describing the camels.
rows.anchor: ومعناه الإشارة إلى ما يعرفه كل أحد من أن الحمد ما هو مثله في قول لبيد يصف العير وأتنه

rows.speaker: لبيد
rows.claim: Labīd’s line, cited as linguistic evidence, uses al-ʿirāk for the camels pressing together at the watering place.
rows.anchor: في قول لبيد يصف العير وأتنه : وأرسلها العراك ولم يذدها

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī calls the exhaustive interpretation of al-ḥamdu a mistaken assumption held by many.
rows.anchor: حتى قال والاستغراق الذي يتوهمه كثير من الناس وهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some tie the generic reading to the Muʿtazilī account that human actions belong to their agents; al-Ālūsī replies that good acts still depend on God’s enabling and empowering.
rows.anchor: فقيل : إنه مبني على مسألة خلق الأعمال فإن أفعال العباد لما كانت مخلوقة لهم عند المعتزلة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Ālūsī rejects arguments that the generic article means only the perfect kind or that a verbal noun cannot convey exhaustive scope; context can make either reading exhaustive.
rows.anchor: ورد بأن اختصاص الجنس يستلزم اختصاص أفراده أيضا

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī paraphrases the phrase as we praise God with a praise, then treats إياك نعبد as an answer explaining how that praise is performed.
rows.anchor: لما كان معناه نحمد الله حمدا كان إخبارا عن ثبوت حمد غير معين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Ālūsī prefers an exhaustive reading here: the sūra’s encompassing attributes of lordship, mercy, and sovereignty support all praise belonging to God, and the shift to إياك نعبد marks a new address rather than an explanation.
rows.anchor: لأن الكلام الأول جار على المدح للغائب بسبب استحقاقه كل الحمد والثاني جار على الحكاية عن نفس الحامد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī’s statement in 64:1 that sovereignty and praise belong exclusively to God supports a comprehensive reading, though the present context gives further reason to include every instance of praise.
rows.anchor: فقال في قوله تعالى : { له الملك وله الحمد } قدم الظرفان ليدل بتقديمهما على معنى اختصاص الملك والحمد

rows.speaker: أبو العباس المرسي
rows.claim: Al-Mursī says the article is covenantal because God praised Himself eternally on behalf of creatures unable to encompass His praise, supported by the prophetic supplication that He is as He praised Himself.
rows.anchor: قلت لابن النحاس ما تقول في الألف واللام في الحمد أجنسية هي أم عهدية

rows.speaker: بعض ساداتنا الصوفية
rows.claim: Some Sufis understand the praise as belonging to God Himself, like sovereignty and creation-command: He is both praiser and praised, and all things are His manifestations.
rows.anchor: أن الحمد لله على حد الكبرياء لله و { أَلاَ لَهُ الخلق والأمر }

rows.speaker: الماتريدي
rows.claim: Al-Māturīdī says God praised Himself in order to teach creatures, and this is fitting because He inherently deserves praise.
rows.anchor: أنه جعل هذا حمدا من الله تعالى لنفسه قال وإنما حمد نفسه ليعلم الخلق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The transmitted and standard reading has al-ḥamdu in the nominative as a subject with lillāhi as its predicate.
rows.anchor: ثم إن الحمد : فيما تواتر مرفوع

rows.speaker: الحسن البصري وزيد بن علي
rows.claim: Al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī and Zayd b. ʿAlī read with the dāl assimilated toward the following lām; Ibrāhīm b. Abla and Bedouins assimilate the reverse way.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الحسن البصري وزيد بن علي ( الحمد لله ) باتباع الدال اللام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This cross-word assimilation is permissible because the two frequently paired words are treated as if they were one word.
rows.anchor: وجاز ذلك استعمالا مع أن الاتباع إنما يكون في كلمة واحدة

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Some prefer Ibrāhīm’s reading because following the first sound is easier than the reverse and because the dāl’s inflection is stronger than the lām’s fixed vowel.
rows.anchor: فقيل قراءة إبراهيم أسهل لأمرين أحدهما : أن اتباع الثاني للأول أيسر

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Others prefer al-Ḥasan’s reading because the second sound more commonly follows the first and the uninflected sound should follow the inflected one.
rows.anchor: وقيل : إن قراءة الحسن أحسن لأن الأكثر جعل الثاني

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī calls Ibrāhīm’s reading أشف, a word that can indicate either greater clarity or greater obscurity.
rows.anchor: وكأنه لتعارض الترجيح قال الزمخشري : وأشف القراءتين قراءة إبراهيم

rows.speaker: هارون بن موسى
rows.claim: Hārūn b. Mūsā reads al-ḥamda in the accusative, a construction common among Arabs for a definite verbal noun with an implied verb such as نحمد.
rows.anchor: وقرأ هارون بن موسى ( الحمد لله ) بالنصب وعامة بني تميم وكثير من العرب ينصبون المصادر بالألف واللام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The implied verb for the accusative is in the first-person plural, matching naʿbudu and nastaʿīn and the humility of worship, rather than a majestic first-person singular.
rows.anchor: قدروه نحمد بنون الجماعة لأنه مقول على ألسنة العباد ومناسب لنعبد ونستعين

rows.speaker: الغزالي
rows.claim: Al-Ghazālī interprets the congregational prayer report as the worshippers speaking collectively in the first-person plural.
rows.anchor: صلاة الجماعة تفضل صلاة الفذ بسبع وعشرين درجة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The nominative reading is strongest because the nominal sentence, in this context, conveys settled and enduring praise rather than a renewed act of praising.
rows.anchor: وأرفع القراءات قراءة الرفع لدلالة الجملة الاسمية على الثبوت والدوام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Grammarians may treat an underlying verbal form as the source construction for verbal nouns, but here the nominative form answers the rhetorical need for an established state.
rows.anchor: إن أصل هذا المصدر النصب لأن المصادر أحداث متعلقة بمحالها

rows.speaker: معظم العلماء
rows.claim: Most scholars consider الحمد لله informative: otherwise God’s possession of the praised qualities would begin only when the speaker utters the praise.
rows.anchor: اختلف في جملة الحمد هل هي إخبارية أم إنشائية ؟ فالذي عليه معظم العلماء أنها إخبارية

rows.speaker: ابن الهمام
rows.claim: Ibn al-Humām argues that ḥamd is performative because it manifests qualities rather than establishing them, so praise need not be informative.
rows.anchor: وذكر أن ما ذكر باطل لأن اللازم من المقارنة انتفاء وصف الواصف لا الاتصاف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Ālūsī sides with the majority: the sentence informs that God deserves praise, while a believer who says it intending reverent description is rightly called a praiser.
rows.anchor: والذي ارتضيه أنها إخبارية كما عليه المعظم ويد الله تعالى مع الجماعة والمراد الإخبار بأن الله تعالى مستحق الحمد

rows.speaker: داود
rows.claim: In a report, David asks how to thank God when gratitude itself is among His gifts; God answers that recognizing inability to thank Him is itself gratitude.
rows.anchor: وقد نقل أن داود عليه السلام قال : يا رب كيف أشكرك والشكر من آلائك ؟

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The servants’ contingent praise relates to God without inhering in Him, just as knowledge relates to its objects without becoming part of them.
rows.anchor: المراد تعلق الحمد به تعالى ولا يلزم من التعلق القيام كتعلق العلم بالمعلومات

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Some take the verbal noun in a passive sense, meaning that God is the one praised; because its form allows several construals, early commentators counted forty-two possibilities.
rows.anchor: وقيل إن الحمد مصدر بناء المجهول فيكون الثابت له عز شأنه هو المحمودية

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: A particularly unusual parsing makes the lām causal, so that praise is established for God’s sake.
rows.anchor: وقيل وهو من الغرابة بمكان أن اللام للتعليل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Naming God by His essential name avoids suggesting that He deserves praise only through one particular attribute; entitlement by essence still means entitlement for divine excellence.
rows.anchor: أتى باسم الذات في الحمدلة لئلا يتوهم لو اقتصر على الصفة اختصاص استحقاقه الحمد بوصف دون وصف

rows.speaker: بعض ساداتنا
rows.claim: A Sufi account divides praise from God into praise of His essence, unity, manifestations, qualities, effects, and acts, while creaturely praise varies with knowledge and capacity.
rows.anchor: فإن وجد من الحق وصدر من الوجود المطلق فتارة يكون على الذات بانفرادها ووحدتها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: When the distinction between Creator and creation is considered together, all praise comes from God and returns to Him; there is no praiser or praised one apart from Him.
rows.anchor: وإذا اعتبر الجمع كان الكل منه وإليه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Praise precedes the divine name because the speaker is about to perform the act of praise; in 30:18 the order is reversed for a different purpose.
rows.anchor: وإنما قدم الحمد على الاسم الكريم لاقتضاء المقام مزيد اهتمام به

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rabb originally denotes tarbiya: gradually bringing a thing to the fullness suited to its primordial capacity, from the growth of a young child.
rows.anchor: والرب في الأصل مصدر بمعنى التربية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rabb is explained as an intensive verbal noun, a form of exaggerated agent noun, or—according to Abū Ḥayyān—an agent noun with a deleted alif; one grammatical account is disputed.
rows.anchor: والظاهر أنه من مبالغة اسم الفاعل أو هو اسم فاعل وأصله رأب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rabb is also used for creator, master, king, benefactor, reformer, worshipped one, and companion; tarbiya is the primary sense, with the others best treated as figurative extensions.
rows.anchor: ويطلق أيضا على الخالق والسيد والملك والمنعم والمصلح والمعبود والصاحب

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī interprets rabb here as owner; al-Ālūsī prefers tarbiya because owner would repeat the sense of Mālik yawm al-dīn and gives no clear reason for placing al-Raḥmān al-Raḥīm between them.
rows.anchor: وحمله الزمخشري هنا على معنى المالك ولعل ما اخترناه خير منه

rows.speaker: الطيبي
rows.claim: Al-Ṭībī finds it preferable to intend both meanings of rabb and their shared sense, as a figure of speech can preserve the direct and implied meaning together.
rows.anchor: ما اختاره الطيبي من وجوب حمل الرب على كلا مفهوميه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In ordinary usage rabb is not freely applied to anyone but God unless restricted by an addition or other qualifier; Ibn Ḥilaza’s unqualified poetic usage is rare.
rows.anchor: لا يطلق لغة على غيره تعالى إطلاقا مستفيضا إلا مقيدا بإضافة

rows.speaker: ابن حلزة
rows.claim: Ibn Ḥilaza’s poem calls al-Mundhir rabb, an unusual unqualified application of the title to a human being.
rows.anchor: وقول ابن حلزة في المنذر بن ماء السماء : وهو الرب والشهيد

rows.speaker: النابغة
rows.claim: Al-Nābigha’s verse uses rabb without a qualifier, illustrating a disputed poetic license.
rows.anchor: وجوز بعضهم إطلاقه منكرا كما في قوله النابغة : نحث إلى النعمان حتى نناله

rows.speaker: أبو هريرة
rows.claim: Abū Hurayra reports the Prophet forbidding a person to say feed or perform ablution for your rabb and instructing him to say master or patron; a note in the source calls this report abrogated.
rows.anchor: وروى الشيخان عن أبي هريرة رضي الله تعالى عنه : «لا يقل أحدكم أطعم ربك وضئ ربك

rows.speaker: السيوطي
rows.claim: Al-Suyūṭī interprets the restriction as a legal rather than purely linguistic ban on calling someone other than God rabb.
rows.anchor: واستظهر الإمام السيوطي أن المراد نفي إطلاقه على غيره تعالى شرعا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Joseph’s use of rabb for his master, and the prostration before Joseph, are explained as permissions specific to that earlier time.
rows.anchor: وأجابوا عن قول يوسف عليه السلام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although ʿālamīn is a sound masculine plural, it can cover nonrational beings if the word is restricted to rational creatures, if rational beings predominate, or if the others are treated as signs of knowledge.
rows.anchor: واعترض بأنه يعم العقلاء وغيرهم وعالمون خاص بالعقلاء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The suggestion that ʿālamīn is a unique collective noun on the pattern of sound plurals does not settle its form; the author distinguishes ordinary plurals, collective generics, and collective nouns.
rows.anchor: وقيل : هو اسم جمع على وزن السلامة ولا نظير له

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ʿĀlam means what makes something known and is commonly used for all that God created, including substances and accidents, or for a whole class of beings.
rows.anchor: والعالم كالخاتم اسم لما يعلم به وغلب فيما يعلم به الخالق تعالى شأنه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The term can denote the aggregate or one or more kinds, but it is not normally applied to a single person; in its basic sense every dependent individual is a sign of its Maker.
rows.anchor: ويطلق على مجموع الأجناس وهو الشائع كما يطلق على واحد منها فصاعدا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Each possible thing, great or small, points to the Creator because all depend on the Necessary Being for existence.
rows.anchor: لإمكانه وافتقاره دليل لائح على الصانع المجيد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The definite plural makes the scope of divine lordship explicit across every created kind; singular al-ʿālam might be mistaken for the familiar perceptible world alone.
rows.anchor: وإنما أتى الرب سبحانه بالجمع المعرف لأنه لو أفرد وعرف بلام الاستغراق لم يكن نصا فيه

rows.speaker: الطيبي
rows.claim: Al-Ṭībī answers that singular exhaustive scope could cover individuals yet fail to make the multiplicity of kinds explicit, so the plural is clearer here.
rows.anchor: لكن الغرض استغراق الأجناس المختلفة فلو أفرد وقيل رب العالم

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Some restrict the worlds to rational beings among angels, humans, and jinn; al-Suyūṭī associates this reading with ʿilm, while universal scope fits ʿalāma, sign.
rows.anchor: وبعضهم خص { العالمين } بذوي العلم من الملائكة والثقلين

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Other reported views limit the worlds to jinn and humans, or to humans alone, citing the Qurʾānic uses in 25:1 and 26:165.
rows.anchor: وقيل هم الجن والإنس لقوله تعالى : { لِيَكُونَ للعالمين نذيرا }

rows.speaker: جعفر الصادق
rows.claim: Jaʿfar al-Ṣādiq is reported to identify the worlds as humans; al-Ālūsī says the broader reading suits the context, while human beings are the focal recipients of law and prophecy.
rows.anchor: وهو المنقول عن جعفر الصادق والمأخوذ من بحر أهل البيت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Human beings are described as a synthesis and miniature of the cosmos; reflection on oneself and the earth reveals signs of the Creator.
rows.anchor: ومن تأمل في ذاته وتفكر في صفاته ظهرت له عظمة باريه

rows.speaker: بعض الأخبار
rows.claim: A report says God created one hundred thousand lamps hung from the Throne, with the heavens, earth, and all they contain in a single lamp; only God knows the rest.
rows.anchor: وروي في بعض الأخبار «أن الله تعالى خلق مائة ألف قنديل وعلقها بالعرش

rows.speaker: كعب الأحبار
rows.claim: Kaʿb al-Aḥbār says no one can enumerate the worlds except God, who creates things people do not know and alone knows His hosts.
rows.anchor: وقال كعب الأحبار : لا يحصي عدد العالمين إلا الله تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Every possible being remains under God’s nurture: without the continuing influx of divine support and the removal of every impediment, it would return to nonexistence.
rows.anchor: وما من ذرة من ذرات العوالم إلا وهي في حيطة تربيته سبحانه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because contingent beings need a cause both to begin and to persist, continual divine preservation is itself tarbiya; keeping even indefinitely many possible obstacles absent sustains a thing.
rows.anchor: كما لا يستحق شيء من الممكنات بذاته الوجود ابتداء لا يستحقه بقاء

rows.speaker: بعض العارفين
rows.claim: A mystic observes that God has other servants, but each person has no lord but Him, while God nurtures each as though He had no servant but that person.
rows.anchor: أنه تعالى يملك عبادا غيرك وأنت ليس لك رب سواه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although the sound masculine plural often denotes a small number, the form here hints that all created worlds remain few beside God’s greatness; the plural can also denote many.
rows.anchor: وإنما كان الجمع بالواو والنون مع أنه في المشهور جمع قلة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: For the gnostics, the station of lordship comprises names that call for objects, such as knowing and power, including shared names and creative names directed toward creatures.
rows.anchor: وقد أشار سبحانه وتعالى بقوله : { رب العالمين } إلى حضرة الربوبية التي هي مقام العارفين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Sufi hierarchy distinguishes Rabb, Rahmān, and Allāh: Rahmān encompasses more divine attributes, while Allāh names the highest, all-encompassing station of divinity.
rows.anchor: وأما الفرق بين الرب والرحمن فهو أن الرحمن عندهم اسم لمرتبة اختصت بجميع الأوصاف العلية الإلهية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In this hierarchy, the essence-only manifestation of aḥadiyya is not disclosed to creatures, whereas ulūhiyya manifests the divine in relation to others.
rows.anchor: ومن ثم منع أهل الله تعالى تجلي الأحدية ولم يمنعوا تجلي الألوهية

rows.speaker: أرباب الظاهر
rows.claim: The outward scholars explain why petitioners say yā Rabb: a petitioner seeks what benefits and nurtures him, so calling on the nurturer is especially apt.
rows.anchor: الداعي لا يطلب إلا ما يظنه صلاحا لحاله وتربية لنفسه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Ālūsī’s own Sufi reading is that souls invoke God by the first name through which they acknowledged Him in the primordial covenant.
rows.anchor: أن الأرواح أول ما شنفت آذانها وعطرت أردانها بسماع وصف الربوبية

rows.speaker: الشيخ الأكبر
rows.claim: Ibn ʿArabī’s account says the universal spirit sought its source without knowing that the sought reality was already within it, then recognized God in the station of lordship.
rows.anchor: مما حاصله : أن الله تعالى لما أوجد الكلمة المعبر عنها بالروح الكلي إيجاد إبداع

rows.speaker: الشيخ الأكبر
rows.claim: In Ibn ʿArabī’s account the spirit names God its Rabb; God gives it divine names and attributes to know through existence, while veiling the manner of that gift because the creature cannot bear it.
rows.anchor: فقال : أنت ربي فلم يعرفه إلا في حضرة الربوبية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Opening the sūra’s descriptions with Rabb al-ʿālamīn suits the Prophet’s mission and asks for compassion toward all creatures, since God is their Lord.
rows.anchor: ويعلم منه إشارة سر افتتاح الأوصاف في الفاتحة برب العالمين

rows.speaker: زيد بن علي
rows.claim: Zayd b. ʿAlī is reported to read rabb al-ʿālamīn in the accusative; the author’s preferred parse is an accusative of detachment with an implied verb such as أمدح.
rows.anchor: وقد قرئ ( رب العالمين ) بالنصب ونسب ذلك إلى زيد بن علي

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: One analysis treats the accusative as detachment from the preceding construction, supplying a verb of praise or mention; another says the prior الحمد licenses the construction.
rows.anchor: فقيل نصب على القطع ويقدر العامل هنا أمدح للمقام أو أذكر

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Other proposed governors are the expressed الحمد, a vocative, or a past-tense reading of rabb; al-Ālūsī objects to the first for its syntax and to the latter parses as awkward.
rows.anchor: وقيل بفعل مقدر دل عليه الحمد وليس على التوهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Ālūsī considers accusative detachment the strongest analysis, especially if al-Raḥmān al-Raḥīm is read in the accusative as a substitute rather than an adjective.
rows.anchor: وأهون الأمور عندي أولها بل يكاد يقطع الظاهر بالقطع
